items.label: f03-production-grade-queue
items.front: What five changes make dotnet-ramp's background processing production-grade?
items.back: Persist the queue (DB table or broker); an outbox for state-change-plus-side-effect atomicity; retry with backoff plus a dead-letter path; a stuck detector for Reimbursing older than N minutes; metrics for queue depth, job duration and failures.

items.label: f01-two-layer-authz
items.front: Describe dotnet-ramp's two-layer authorization model for expenses (reads and writes).
items.back: Coarse: [Authorize(Roles=...)] says 'some manager'. Fine: service checks such as EnsureManagesOwner, CanView/List scoping reads to own/team/all by role, and owner-scoped writes via GetOwned. The fine layer is the IDOR defense.

items.label: f04-outbox-test-and-rollback
items.front: How does the critique propose to test and roll back the reimbursement outbox?
items.back: An OutboxEntry is written in the same SaveChanges as the status change and polled by a dispatcher. Test: kill the dispatcher mid-flight, restart, assert exactly-once payment. Rollback: feature-flag the dispatcher and fall back to direct enqueue.

items.label: f02-queue-reliability-table
items.front: Summarize the reliability properties of dotnet-ramp's in-process background queue.
items.back: In-memory, at-most-once: no durability (a crash loses queued and in-flight jobs), no retries, partial idempotency (ProcessReimbursement guards, ProcessReceipt does not), enqueue not transactional with the state change, visibility via logs only.

items.prompt: The outbox redesign writes the status change and an OutboxEntry in one SaveChanges and lets a dispatcher perform the payment with retries. Why does the payment job still have to be idempotent?

choices.text: The outbox delivers exactly-once on its own; idempotency only matters for the receipt job
Delivery becomes at-least-once, so a crash-retry can run the payment twice
Idempotency replaces the transaction; with it the OutboxEntry could be written separately
The dispatcher runs on the request thread, so two requests can enqueue the same entry

choices: The outbox delivers exactly-once on its own; idempotency only matters for the receipt job
Delivery becomes at-least-once, so a crash-retry can run the payment twice
Idempotency replaces the transaction; with it the OutboxEntry could be written separately
The dispatcher runs on the request thread, so two requests can enqueue the same entry

items.explanation: The outbox converts at-most-once into at-least-once; at-least-once plus an idempotent side effect is what gives one payment, which the critique's test (kill the dispatcher mid-flight, restart, assert exactly-once payment) checks.

items.prompt: The same ProcessReimbursement job runs twice for one expense. Why is the second run harmless?

choices.text: It re-checks CanSystemTransition, finds Reimbursed has no legal next edge, and returns
The bounded channel deduplicates identical delegates, so the second copy is never dequeued
QueuedHostedService catches the DomainException that Transition throws and drops the job
It finds the existing PaymentReference and reuses it instead of issuing a new payment

choices: It re-checks CanSystemTransition, finds Reimbursed has no legal next edge, and returns
The bounded channel deduplicates identical delegates, so the second copy is never dequeued
QueuedHostedService catches the DomainException that Transition throws and drops the job
It finds the existing PaymentReference and reuses it instead of issuing a new payment

items.explanation: ProcessReimbursement is idempotent by guard: Reimbursed has no outgoing edge, so the legality re-check fails and it returns without paying again. ProcessReceipt has no such guard.

items.prompt: Finance clicks reimburse; StartReimbursement flips the expense to Reimbursing and then enqueues the payment job. The process crashes before the worker dequeues it. What is the state after restart?

choices.text: Paid twice, because the restart re-runs StartReimbursement for every Reimbursing expense
Stuck in Reimbursing with no payment and nothing that will ever retry it
Reimbursed, because the bounded channel replays its pending jobs on startup
Back in Approved, because the unawaited enqueue never committed the status change

choices: Paid twice, because the restart re-runs StartReimbursement for every Reimbursing expense
Stuck in Reimbursing with no payment and nothing that will ever retry it
Reimbursed, because the bounded channel replays its pending jobs on startup
Back in Approved, because the unawaited enqueue never committed the status change

items.explanation: The status change happens first and the enqueue is neither awaited nor transactional; the queue is in-memory, so the job dies with the process and nothing recovers the expense.

items.prompt: Moving from the singleton DataStore to a scoped, non-thread-safe DbContext, why is the background worker already structurally prepared?

choices.text: The bounded channel runs one job at a time, so a singleton DbContext would be safe there
Jobs run on the request thread, so they share the request's DbContext safely
It opens a fresh DI scope per job, so each job can resolve its own scoped DbContext
BackgroundService resolves every dependency as transient, so lifetimes never matter

choices: The bounded channel runs one job at a time, so a singleton DbContext would be safe there
Jobs run on the request thread, so they share the request's DbContext safely
It opens a fresh DI scope per job, so each job can resolve its own scoped DbContext
BackgroundService resolves every dependency as transient, so lifetimes never matter

items.explanation: DbContext must be scoped; code holding the store in a long-lived field would break, but the worker already calls CreateScope() per job, mimicking a per-request scope.

items.prompt: The background channel is full (capacity 100) when a request calls EnqueueAsync. What happens?

choices.text: The producer waits until the worker frees a slot
EnqueueAsync throws immediately and the request returns 503
The oldest queued job is dropped to make room
The channel grows past capacity and memory use rises without limit

choices: The producer waits until the worker frees a slot
EnqueueAsync throws immediately and the request returns 503
The oldest queued job is dropped to make room
The channel grows past capacity and memory use rises without limit

items.explanation: BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait gives backpressure: producers wait instead of growing memory without limit.

A background job recalculates every flag nightly and stores the result

choices.text: It still returns early when the user does not exist, so timing can differ
The constant-time comparison is only applied to the admin accounts
PBKDF2 with 100k iterations runs in variable time for different passwords
The salt is stored beside the hash, which leaks whether the user exists

items.explanation: PBKDF2 + per-user salt + constant-time compare is done right; the early return on a missing user is the gap to investigate.

Everything, because unknown roles are treated as administrators

Only their own expenses, via the owner-scoped GetOwned query

Switch the store to a scoped lifetime; each request then gets its own copy
Wrap every service method in one global lock held around the whole DataStore singleton

items.explanation: R4 is a check-then-act gap (rare double-submit). The suggested start: state the assumption, add a concurrency token on Expense, reject stale writes; the test is two concurrent submits giving one 409.

Users is a ConcurrentDictionary, so the lookup can return a torn read under load
GetValueOrDefault throws once an employee is deleted, failing the whole list response
It leaks the employee's password hash into the response DTO
